title: Convergence properties of generalized Benders decomposition
contribution: Two convergence properties of GBD: one cut suffices when the NLP relaxation gap is zero, and on nonconvex problems GBD may miss the global optimum and even a local minimum (abstract of the report version).
problem_entry: Two open questions about the convergence of GBD, an algorithm for mixed-integer linear and nonlinear programs (abstract).
key_idea: (i) A proof that a MINLP formulation with zero NLP relaxation gap needs only one Benders cut, the one at the optimal solution; (ii) a demonstration that GBD on nonconvex problems need not reach the global optimum or even a local minimum, because every local optimum of the NLP gives rise to a local optimum of the projected Benders problem (abstract).
assumptions: Convexity is the hypothesis whose absence breaks GBD's guarantee (abstract).
proof_devices: Proof of one-cut convergence for formulations with zero NLP relaxation gap (abstract; proof not read)
Failure mechanism: local optima of the NLP map to local optima of the projected problem; illustrated by examples (abstract; examples not read)
positioning: The S013 reference list (Springer landing page) cites this paper, so the nonconvex-GBD result was in view when branch-and-reduce was written (metadata).
writing: States the lesson in one sentence: tight formulations matter for integer programs (abstract).
limits_future: The negative result is a limit of GBD itself: no global guarantee on nonconvex problems (abstract).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: failure case of the standard decomposition, explained, before the fix
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: new: GBD shown to stall at non-global, even non-local points on nonconvex problems, with the mechanism stated; S064 shows the same move for Benders on trivial TDTSPs.

transferable: Pair a positive convergence result with a failure class and name the mechanism of failure (here: local optima of the subproblem become local optima of the projected problem) (abstract).

quotes.text: First, it is proved that a mixed integer nonlinear programming formulation with zero nonlinear programming relaxation gap requires only one Benders cut in order to converge, namely the cut corresponding to the optimal solution.

Second, it is demonstrated that the application of generalized Benders decomposition to nonconvex problems does not always lead to the global optimum for these problems; it may not even lead to a local minimum.
